content: On July 28, 2006, approximately 2,500 chickens died at the Dongbang poultry farm in Xaythany district, Laos, due to the H5N1 virus. This marked the country's first significant outbreak since 2004. The government of Laos responded promptly by culling all chickens on the farm, disinfecting the premises, and imposing movement restrictions within a five-kilometer surveillance zone, according to Wantanee Kalpravidh, the FAO regional coordinator for Avian Influenza Projects. On August 5, 2006, a German zoo and a Vietnam theme park reported highly pathogenic H5N1 infections in their birds. By August 10, experts expressed concern over Indonesia's inadequate control measures, which had led to widespread outbreaks across the densely populated archipelago. Indonesia, which reported its first human case in July 2005, had since experienced an unparalleled rise in cases, with 56 confirmed human infections and 44 fatalities. Globally, 236 cases of H5N1 infection had been confirmed in 10 countries since late 2003, with 138 deaths. On August 12, 2006, Cambodia reported its second bird flu outbreak of the year in Prey Veng province, where the H5N1 virus had killed a boy in April. Over 1,300 ducks died, but no human infections were reported. Senior Agriculture Ministry official Nou Muth confirmed the resurgence of bird flu in the region. On August 18, 2006, the World Health Organization (WHO) updated its recommendations for H5N1 avian influenza vaccine strains for the first time since 2004. Experts noted the virus's rapid evolution into a complex network of clades and subclades, complicating vaccine development. Michael Osterholm emphasized that a strain-specific vaccine would be necessary in the event of a pandemic. On August 25, 2006, the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy (CIDRAP) reported on a new U.S. government website providing public access to data on wild bird testing for H5N1 as part of a national surveillance plan. The program aimed to collect 75,000 to 100,000 samples from wild birds and 50,000 environmental samples in 2006. On September 7, 2006, Indonesian officials confirmed that a 14-year-old girl who died in June had been infected with bird flu. This case was identified during routine surveillance of blood samples from individuals with flu-like symptoms. Health Minister Siti Fadillah Supari announced a policy change, allowing Indonesia to confirm infections locally after two positive tests, rather than relying on WHO laboratories. On September 13, 2006, Sudanese authorities announced that chicken samples from southern Sudan tested positive for the deadly H5N1 virus. On September 25, 2006, a 21-year-old woman in East Java, Indonesia, was hospitalized with H5N1 symptoms. She was the sister of an 11-year-old boy who had died from the virus on September 18. Both were believed to have been exposed to dead poultry in their household. On September 27, 2006, the WHO confirmed a resurgence of highly pathogenic H5N1 in domestic chickens near Aswan, Upper Egypt. Animals within a one-kilometer radius of the infection site were culled and buried to prevent further spread. On October 4, 2006, U.S. government inspectors increased vigilance against avian flu following scares in Pennsylvania and Maryland. The USDA and DOI confirmed the presence of H5N1 subtypes in wild mallard ducks in Pennsylvania but ruled out the highly pathogenic strain circulating in Asia, Europe, and Africa. The low pathogenic strain posed no threat to humans. On October 11, 2006, Egyptian authorities confirmed the country's first human case of highly pathogenic H5N1 since May. A woman hospitalized on October 4 tested positive for the virus. On October 16, 2006, a 67-year-old Indonesian woman died of bird flu, marking the country's 54th fatality from the virus. On October 31, 2006, a 39-year-old Egyptian woman died of bird flu, the first case in Egypt since May. On November 2, 2006, a dog in Thailand succumbed to bird flu, raising concerns about the potential for pets to contract and spread the disease to humans. On November 13, 2006, Indonesia confirmed two new H5N1 cases: a 35-year-old woman and a 30-month-old boy, both of whom developed symptoms in early November. On December 12, 2006, South Korea reported its third major H5N1 outbreak in less than three weeks, all in North Cholla province. Over one million birds were culled to contain the virus. The U.S. government continued to prepare for a potential influenza pandemic, with federal departments and agencies developing comprehensive preparedness plans.
